subject: Medieval History
sub_topic: Revenue system — Zabt system origins under Sher Shah

concepts.name: Zabt System: Definition, Origins, and Nomenclature
key_dimensions: Distinction between 'Zabt' as a measurement-based system vs. other revenue systems (batai, nasaq, kankut)
Whether Zabt originated under Sher Shah or was merely systematized — the historiographical debate
The term 'Zabti' used interchangeably with 'Ain-i-Dahsala' later under Akbar — UPSC trap on attribution
Role of Todar Mal in later codifying what Sher Shah initiated — continuity vs. innovation question

concepts.name: Land Measurement (Patta and Qabuliyat) under Sher Shah
key_dimensions: Patta: the document issued to the peasant stating the amount of land and revenue due — its legal significance
Qabuliyat: the bond/deed of agreement signed by the peasant — nature of contractual obligation
How this system created a direct state-peasant relationship bypassing intermediaries
UPSC trap: Confusing Patta-Qabuliyat with later Mughal documentation systems under Akbar

concepts.name: Measurement Unit: Sikandari Gaz vs. Ilahi Gaz
key_dimensions: Sher Shah's use of Sikandari Gaz (yard of Sikandar Lodi) as the standard unit of land measurement
Difference between Sikandari Gaz and Ilahi Gaz introduced under Akbar — common UPSC confusion
Standardization of measurement as a reform tool to reduce local manipulation by revenue officials
How inconsistent measurement units before Sher Shah led to revenue evasion and peasant exploitation

concepts.name: Share of Produce (Raj Bhag): Rate and Determination
key_dimensions: Sher Shah fixed the state's share at one-third (1/3) of the total produce — significance of this rate
Comparison with Delhi Sultanate norms (Alauddin Khilji's half-produce demand) — reform dimension
Whether payment was accepted in cash or kind — flexibility and its administrative implications
UPSC trap: Confusing Sher Shah's one-third share with Akbar's later rate variations under the Ain-i-Dahsala

concepts.name: Classification of Land: Polaj, Parauti, Chachar, Banjar
key_dimensions: Four-fold classification of agricultural land under Sher Shah's revenue framework
Polaj (land under continuous cultivation) vs. Parauti (fallow land temporarily out of use) — differential taxation
Chachar (fallow for 3-4 years) and Banjar (uncultivated for 5+ years) — reduced revenue rates as incentive
UPSC trap: This classification is often attributed solely to Akbar's Ain; its origins in Sher Shah's system must be noted

concepts.name: Role of Amin, Muqaddam, and Patwari in Revenue Collection
key_dimensions: Amin as the revenue assessor/supervisor — his function distinct from the qanungo and patwari
Muqaddam (village headman) and Patwari (village accountant) as local intermediaries in Sher Shah's system
Sher Shah's attempt to make officials accountable through checks — significance for administrative reform
UPSC trap: Confusing Amin with Amil (revenue collector under Akbar) — different roles in different periods

concepts.name: Schedule of Rates (Ray): Crop-wise Revenue Assessment
key_dimensions: Sher Shah introduced a schedule (ray) listing different crops and their respective revenue rates
Differentiation between cash crops (cotton, sugarcane, indigo) and food crops in revenue calculation
This crop-based differentiation as a precursor to Akbar's more elaborate Ain-i-Dahsala schedules
How crop schedules helped standardize assessment across provinces — reducing arbitrary demands

concepts.name: Sher Shah's Revenue System vs. Alauddin Khilji's Revenue Reforms: Comparison
key_dimensions: Alauddin measured land and fixed revenue at 50% of produce — coercive model vs. Sher Shah's 33% model
Alauddin's system was city/army-centric; Sher Shah's aimed at peasant welfare and agricultural productivity
Both used direct state-to-peasant assessment but differed in intent, rate, and administrative apparatus
UPSC frequently tests this comparison to distinguish reform motivations across medieval rulers

concepts.name: Continuity from Sher Shah to Akbar: Todar Mal's Role
key_dimensions: Todar Mal served under Sher Shah before becoming Akbar's revenue minister — institutional continuity
Ain-i-Dahsala (Ten-Year Settlement, 1580) as an elaboration and systematization of Sher Shah's Zabt principles
Key differences: Akbar introduced 10-year averaging of prices; Sher Shah used current year assessments
UPSC trap: Erroneously attributing the origin of Zabt entirely to Akbar/Todar Mal, ignoring Sher Shah's foundational role

concepts.name: Sher Shah's Use of Kankut (Crop Estimation) alongside Zabt
key_dimensions: Kankut: estimation of yield by inspection of standing crops — used in areas where measurement was impractical
How Sher Shah used Zabt (measurement) as the primary method but retained Kankut as a supplementary tool
Batai (sharing at threshing floor) as a third method — why Sher Shah preferred Zabt over Batai
UPSC trap: Treating these three methods as mutually exclusive rather than contemporaneously used alternatives

concepts.name: Welfare Provisions and Peasant Protection Measures
key_dimensions: Sher Shah's prohibition on soldiers destroying crops or foraging from peasant fields during military campaigns
Provision of taccavi (agricultural loans) during famines or crop failures — state responsibility dimension
How relief measures integrated with the Zabt system to maintain peasant solvency and continuity of revenue
Significance in the context of benevolent vs. extractive medieval state — a common UPSC analytical question

concepts.name: Administrative Geography: Sarkars, Parganas, and Revenue Units
key_dimensions: Sher Shah's division of the empire into Sarkars subdivided into Parganas as the basic revenue units
Shiqdar (law and order) and Amin (revenue) at the Pargana level — dual administrative control
How this territorial administrative structure enabled the effective implementation of the Zabt system
UPSC trap: Confusing Sher Shah's administrative units with Akbar's later formalization of the same structure

concepts.name: Currency Standardization and Its Link to Cash Revenue Collection
key_dimensions: Sher Shah's introduction of the silver Rupiya (Rupee) and copper Dam — standardized currency system
How currency standardization was a prerequisite for shifting from in-kind to cash revenue payments
The Dam as the unit for smaller transactions in village-level revenue settlements
UPSC frequently links Sher Shah's monetary reforms with his revenue reforms as a package of economic modernization

concepts.name: Role of the Qanungo in Record-Keeping and Revenue Continuity
key_dimensions: Qanungo: a hereditary record-keeper at the Pargana level who maintained historical revenue data
How Qanungos provided institutional memory that enabled consistent assessment across revenue years
Sher Shah's use of Qanungo records to cross-check Amin's assessments — a check-and-balance mechanism
UPSC trap: Conflating Qanungo with Patwari — both keep records but at different administrative levels

concepts.name: Sher Shah's Revenue System: Impact on Peasantry vs. Intermediary (Zamindar) Class
key_dimensions: Sher Shah's direct state-peasant relationship as a deliberate weakening of intermediary power
How Patta-Qabuliyat system reduced the zamindars' ability to manipulate revenue assessments
Tension between centralization (Sher Shah's goal) and local power structures (zamindars' resistance)
Long-term significance: this model influenced Mughal debates on zamindari rights throughout the 16th–17th centuries

concepts.name: Sources for Understanding Sher Shah's Revenue System: Abbas Khan Sarwani and Abul Fazl
key_dimensions: Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi by Abbas Khan Sarwani — primary Persian source, written under Akbar, its biases and limitations
Abul Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari as a comparative source that describes evolved Mughal revenue practices rooted in Sher Shah
UPSC trap: Over-relying on Mughal sources to describe Sher Shah's system may introduce retrospective distortion
How the absence of dedicated contemporary revenue manuals from Sher Shah's reign complicates precise reconstruction

concepts.name: Comparison of Zabt System with Ryotwari (British-era) System: Structural Parallels
key_dimensions: Both Zabt and Ryotwari establish a direct state-cultivator relationship bypassing intermediaries
Key difference: Zabt was based on measured area and fixed rates; Ryotwari involved annual individual assessment
UPSC sometimes tests long-run continuities and structural similarities in Indian revenue history across medieval and colonial periods
Danger of over-drawing parallels — Zabt lacked the permanent settlement character and judicial enforcement of Ryotwari

concepts.name: Sher Shah's Revenue System and Its Short Duration: Why It Did Not Fully Institutionalize
key_dimensions: Sher Shah ruled only from 1540–1545 (5 years) — insufficient time for complete imperial institutionalization
His successors (Islam Shah, etc.) lacked capacity to maintain the system's integrity
Why Akbar had to reinvent/re-implement these reforms 30+ years later rather than inheriting a working system
Historiographical debate: Was Sher Shah's system a 'blueprint' or an 'experiment'? — tests higher-order UPSC analytical skills
